Figure 1: Where each figure’s data comes from. Cylinders are the cached Public Health Scotland files, rounded boxes are silos (coloured by stage of the patient’s journey: blue front door, green ward, orange back door), hexagons are alignments, and the grey boxes at the bottom are the figures. Edge labels say what each step keeps or sums.





Two things the diagram makes visible that the code alone doesn’t. The ward only exists by quarter, so it forces the other two silos up to its grain before they can meet it; and each figure has its own alignment, so the monthly chart can use all 122 months, while the three-silo charts are limited to the 21 quarters the ward covers.

title: Front door, ward, back door: the whole system in one script
section: How alignment works, and what it catches
text:
How alignment works, and what it catches


Code
flow_m <- align_silos(
  front_door = front_door_scot_m,   # A&E, Scotland, by month
  back_door  = back_door_scot_m,    # delayed discharges, Scotland, by month
  by = "month"
)


For the monthly Scotland system, alignment keeps 122 months, July 2016 to August 2026, and drops 108 A&E months that have no delayed-discharge record (that series starts later). The drop is reported, not silent.
If a silo is ambiguous, for example because a month appears twice after a careless append, alignment stops instead of drawing a plausible wrong chart:


Error: silo 'back_door' has 1 key(s) with more than one row; aggregate it to
one row per month first

title: Front door, ward, back door: the whole system in one script
text:
First drafts of the figures
These are the agent’s drafts, made without a group. Each one is a set of decisions the group can overturn.

One silo against another, by name


Code
ggplot() +
  geom_path(aes(x = flow_m$back_door$delayed_beds, y = flow_m$front_door$pct_4h),
            linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.5, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(x = flow_m$back_door$delayed_beds, y = flow_m$front_door$pct_4h,
                 colour = flow_m$front_door$month), size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(trans = "date", labels = scales::label_date("%Y")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = \(y) paste0(y, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Back door: beds occupied by delayed discharges (daily average)",
       y = "Front door: A&E patients seen within 4 hours",
       colour = NULL, title = "Back door against front door") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"), legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 2: Scotland, monthly. Every aesthetic names its silo: flow\(back_door on x, flow\)front_door on y and in colour. Colour runs from the earliest month (dark) to the latest (yellow).





This is the same chart as the earlier page’s cross-silo view, drawn from separate silos rather than a joined table. Nothing about the picture changes. What changes is the code a reader copies: it names the two parts of the system on every line.


The whole system on one page


Code
stages <- c(
  front_door = "Front door: A&E patients seen within 4 hours (%)",
  ward       = "Ward: acute beds occupied (%)",
  back_door  = "Back door: beds occupied by delayed discharges (daily average)"
)

whole_system <- bind_rows(
  front_door = tibble(quarter = flow_q$front_door$quarter, value = flow_q$front_door$pct_4h),
  ward       = tibble(quarter = flow_q$ward$quarter,       value = flow_q$ward$occupancy),
  back_door  = tibble(quarter = flow_q$back_door$quarter,  value = flow_q$back_door$delayed_beds),
  .id = "stage"
) |>
  mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = names(stages), labels = stages))

ggplot(whole_system, aes(quarter, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2", size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ stage, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "One patient journey, three publications") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, face = "bold"))








Figure 3: Scotland, quarterly. One panel per stage of the patient’s journey, from the front door down to the back door, sharing the time axis. The y scales are free because the measures are in different units.





Read from top to bottom, the panels follow a patient in and out of hospital. Over these 21 quarters, acute occupancy ran from 80% to 89%, and it was above 85% in 17 of them. 85% is often quoted as the level above which hospitals start to struggle to admit promptly. The line between the panels is the argument the chart exists to make: the front door’s figure is partly made at the back door, and the ward is where they meet.


Front door against ward, board by board


Code
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = flow_hb_q$ward$occupancy, y = flow_hb_q$front_door$pct_4h,
                 alpha = flow_hb_q$ward$quarter),
             colour = "#0072B2", size = 1.6) +
  scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.15, 0.9), trans = "date", guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = \(y) paste0(y, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Ward: acute beds occupied",
       y = "Front door: A&E patients seen within 4 hours",
       title = "Fuller wards, slower front doors?") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 4: Each point is one health board in one quarter. x comes from the ward silo and y from the front-door silo, aligned on board and quarter. Older quarters are fainter.





This uses 14 boards with both an emergency department and acute beds. Boards differ in size, case mix and geography, so a cloud like this mixes differences between boards with changes within each board over time. Separating the two is the obvious next step for a group, by faceting by board or by drawing one path per board.

title: Front door, ward, back door: the whole system in one script
text:
Candidate mappings (the group chooses)
Candidates (the group chooses) - nhs-whole-system:
  silos:          front_door (A&E), ward (acute beds), back_door (delayed discharges)
  grain:          board x month (two silos) or board x quarter (all three)
  position x/y:   any silo's measure against any other's, after align_silos()
  facet:          stage (journey order), or board
  colour/alpha:   time; or a third silo's measure (e.g. delayed beds on the ward plot)
  silo as data:   bind_rows(.id = "stage") turns "which part of the system" into a variable
Questions for the group:

Is the $ version clearer, or just shorter? The test is whether someone new to the data can say, from the code alone, which parts of the system the chart connects.
Journey names or team names? front_door is vivid but informal. Some teams would rather see the publication name.
Should the helper be visible? It could live in a shared script so the session sees only the $ plots, or be written live as part of the lesson.
What belongs between the ward and the back door? Length of stay and discharges by day of the week are both published and both sit on the same path.

title: Front door, ward, back door: the whole system in one script
text:
What the data can’t say
These are aggregate totals by board and month or quarter. They can’t follow a patient, so they can’t show that the person waiting in A&E was waiting for a bed held by a delayed discharge. The three measures share drivers, including an ageing population, winter, staffing and the pandemic, that could move them together without any causal chain. The four-hour figure includes patients who were never admitted. Acute occupancy is an average over a quarter and a whole board, so it hides the days and hospitals that were full. The three-silo record is only 21 quarters, starting late in the first pandemic year, which is too short to separate a trend from a relationship. Bed definitions and delay definitions are set nationally and can change; a change in definition would look like a change in the system.






TipReproducing this page: download the whole pipeline as one R script





Download whole-system.R (annotated, about 300 lines). It runs every step on this page from start to finish: it fetches the data (or uses the cached copies in data/), builds the three silos, defines align_silos(), sums to quarters, does the three alignments, shows the duplicated-month check, saves the three figures to figures/, and prints the numbers quoted above. Run it from the repository root, or from any empty folder:
Rscript whole-system.R
It needs only the tidyverse. It was checked on 2026-10-13 by running it in an empty folder, where it downloaded all three files and reproduced every number on this page.
The data comes from the Public Health Scotland open data portal, under the Open Government Licence v3:

phs-ae-monthly.csv: Monthly A&E activity and waiting times.
phs-delayed-discharge.csv: Delayed discharges in NHSScotland.
phs-beds-quarterly.csv: NHS beds information in Scotland, beds by board of treatment and specialty. This page uses the All Acute rows at board level (where Location equals HB). Pulled on 2026-10-13, it runs from October–December 2020 to October–December 2025, and quarters are calendar quarters.

Some download links carry the release month, so they go out of date. If a download fails, take the current link from the dataset page and update the sources table at the top of the script. The page itself also reads phs-health-boards.csv (health board codes and labels), which the script doesn’t need.
Cite Public Health Scotland as the source.

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
section: How this session works: a scientific supergroup
text:
How this session works: a scientific supergroup
The room is too big for everyone to make every decision, so this session runs as a masterclass in the scientific supergroup format. Three people, each with different expertise, work through one problem together in front of the room. No one needs every skill; the point is what the combination can do. The format is described on the KT&B site: Scientific Supergroups.









Role
Who
What they bring




Domain expert
Chelsi Slotten
Names the domain and the question. Says what matters, what’s plausible, and what the data is missing.


Analyst / statistician
Ozan Evkaya
Advises on how to show the data and how to read it: the right summary, the right comparison, and the uncertainty.


AI wrangler
Jon Minton

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
1. The domain
Domain: archaeology or biodiversity.
Question: the session opened with the statistician’s question, how the four plant categories are spread around the region. It became the domain expert’s: “I’d love to see that start and end date against the founder crops, because this is a period where we have a shift from hunter-gatherer to agriculture.”
Why it matters: eight “founder crops” have long been thought to be the bedrock of Neolithic farming in Southwest Asia. When and where they appear in the archaeological record bears on how the shift from hunting and gathering to farming happened.

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
2. Finding a TidyTuesday dataset
We searched the TidyTuesday yearly indexes (2018–2026) for archaeology and biodiversity. The search found four archaeology weeks and 13 biodiversity weeks, including National Park Species, Global Invasive Species, Extinct Plants (IUCN Red List), AVONET birds, AmphibiaWeb and the Portal Project. The archaeology weeks were:



Week
What it is




2023-04-18
Neolithic Founder Crops: plant remains from archaeological sites in Southwest Asia


2026-06-30
Wreck Inventory of Ireland: shipwrecks


2024-02-06
UNESCO World Heritage Sites


2019-08-13
Roman Emperors (history more than archaeology)



Chosen: Neolithic Founder Crops, TidyTuesday 2023-04-18 (founder_crops.csv), which sits between the two domains: archaeology, through plant remains. Why: participants suggested World Heritage Sites and Australian Frogs, and the room briefly settled on frogs. The domain expert then chose plant remains, a topic the domain expert was better informed to talk about.






TipReproducing this page





Everything runs from CSVs cached in this repository’s data/ folder. To refresh from source:
# sh scripts/workshop r scripts/tt_fetch.R 2023-04-18
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2023/2023-04-18/founder_crops.csv",
  "data/tt-2023-04-18-founder_crops.csv")
Packages: tidyverse. Source: Joe Roe’s research compendium, The “Neolithic Founder Crops” in Southwest Asia, for the paper Revisiting the concept of the “Neolithic Founder Crops” in southwest Asia, via TidyTuesday 2023-04-18. Licence: none stated in the TidyTuesday readme.
The basemap (round 3) is Natural Earth’s 1:50m country outlines, public domain:
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvkelso/natural-earth-vector/master/geojson/ne_50m_admin_0_countries.geojson",
  "data/ne-50m-admin0-countries.geojson")
Packages for the basemap and the interactive version: sf, plotly.





Code
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

crops <- read_csv("../../data/tt-2023-04-18-founder_crops.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

n_site_phases <- n_distinct(crops$site_name, crops$phase_code)
n_dup_keys <- sum(duplicated(crops[c("site_name", "phase_code", "taxon_source")]))
phase_prop_sum <- crops |>
  summarise(total = sum(prop), .by = c(site_name, phase_code)) |>
  pull(total)

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
3. What the data holds
Grain: one row per plant taxon found in one phase of one site. The table has 4490 rows and 24 columns. It covers 135 sites and 240 site phases (a phase is one period of occupation at a site). 8 rows repeat a site, phase and taxon combination.








Variable
Type (grammar terms)
Notes




latitude, longitude
continuous
One point per site; Southwest Asia


age_start, age_end
continuous, reversed
Years before 1950 (BP), so larger means older. Phases run from 14,111 to 1,950 BP


phase, phase_code
discrete, 240 codes
Site-specific names (e.g. “PPNB”, “Abu Hureyra 1”), not a shared timeline


category
discrete, 4 levels
Fruits/nuts, Grasses, Pulses, Wild plants


founder_crop
discrete, 9 levels
The eight founder crops, plus “wheat” where the species wasn’t identified


family, genus, taxon
discrete, many levels
63 families, 256 taxa


n
continuous, count
Specimens in the sample. Long right tail, up to 127,336,210


prop
continuous, 0–1
This taxon’s share of its site phase’s sample



Missing values:

founder_crop is empty for 3,433 rows (76%). Here empty means “not a founder crop”, which carries information; it isn’t lost data.
category is not recorded for 7 rows. This wasn’t discussed; on the maps, these rows aren’t drawn.
Within a site phase, the prop values add up to a median of 0.81, not 1. This wasn’t discussed; none of the charts uses prop.

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
4. Design decisions
Each decision is recorded as a decision: what was considered, what was chosen, and why. The decision log grows as the session goes:










#
Decision
Options considered
Chosen
Why




1
Position
Points, or two-dimensional bins (the statistician’s suggestion)
Longitude on x, latitude on y: a map of the sites
The statistician wanted to see how the four plant categories are spread around the region


2
What distinguishes the points
Category on shape, colour, or both
Plant category on both colour and shape
To tell the four categories apart on the map


3
What distinguishes the points, revised
Founder crop, genus or taxon
Founder crop on both colour and shape, in place of plant category
Round 1 showed no clear pattern by category. The domain expert expected differences at a finer level, because different fruits, nuts and grasses grow in different environments. “Species” isn’t a column; the facilitator meant founder crop


4
Context for the points
Basemap or none
A basemap of country outlines, plus an interactive version to consider
A participant asked for a coastline, to see where in the world the sites are. The facilitator added interactivity


5
From place to time
None discussed
Start and end date (x) against founder crop (y)
The domain expert: the period covers the shift from hunting and gathering to farming


6
Direction of time
Older on the right (default) or on the left
Older on the left
To read from when the founder crops first arrive




Round 1: where the sites are, by plant category
The group asked for the sites by longitude and latitude, with plant category mapped to both colour and shape.
# specs/01-site-map-category.yml
data: tt-2023-04-18-founder_crops   # grain: one row per taxon in one phase of one site
mapping:
  x: longitude
  y: latitude
  colour: category
  shape: category
layers:
  - geom: point


Code
ggplot(crops, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = category, shape = category)) +
  geom_point()








Figure 1





What the render showed: the sites form a band across Southwest Asia, but the categories can’t be told apart. Each row is one taxon in one phase, so every site has many rows at the same position: 132 locations carry 4490 points, and the symbols are drawn on top of each other. The 7 rows with no category have no shape, so they aren’t drawn, and “NA” appears in the legend with no symbol. In response, the group kept the map and changed the variable on colour and shape to founder crop (round 2).


Round 2: the same map, by founder crop
The group kept the map and put founder crop on colour and shape in place of plant category. The spec check warned before rendering: “ggplot2’s default shape palette has 6 shapes, so founder_crop’s other 3 levels would be dropped.”
# specs/02-site-map-founder-crop.yml
data: tt-2023-04-18-founder_crops   # grain: one row per taxon in one phase of one site
mapping:
  x: longitude
  y: latitude
  colour: founder_crop
  shape: founder_crop
layers:
  - geom: point


Code
ggplot(crops, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = founder_crop, shape = founder_crop)) +
  geom_point()








Figure 2





What the render showed: only the first six crops in alphabetical order are drawn (barley to flax). Lentil, pea and unidentified wheat get no shape, so they are missing from the map but still listed in the legend. The 3,433 rows that aren’t founder crops have no shape either. In all, 3,762 of 4,490 rows are not drawn. The stacking from round 1 remains: at most sites the symbols overlap. In response, the facilitator asked for the same map drawn on a basemap, and for an interactive version to be considered (round 3).


Round 3: on a basemap
The facilitator asked for the round 2 map to be redrawn on a basemap. No map package was installed, so the basemap is Natural Earth’s 1:50m country outlines (public domain), downloaded at the facilitator’s explicit request. The spec schema has no slot for a layer with its own data, so the basemap layer names its data inside the layer. Three choices in this spec were made by the agent and can be changed on request: light grey land, white borders, and a view cropped to the sites plus one degree on each side.
# specs/03-site-map-founder-crop-basemap.yml
data: tt-2023-04-18-founder_crops   # grain: one row per taxon in one phase of one site
mapping:
  x: longitude
  y: latitude
  colour: founder_crop
  shape: founder_crop
layers:
  - geom: sf
    data: ne-50m-admin0-countries.geojson
    inherit.aes: false
    fill: grey92
    colour: white
  - geom: point
coords: "coord_sf(xlim = range(longitude) + c(-1, 1), ylim = range(latitude) + c(-1, 1))"


Code
world <- sf::read_sf("../../data/ne-50m-admin0-countries.geojson")

p03 <- ggplot(crops, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = founder_crop, shape = founder_crop)) +
  geom_sf(data = world, inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey92", colour = "white") +
  geom_point() +
  coord_sf(xlim = range(crops$longitude) + c(-1, 1), ylim = range(crops$latitude) + c(-1, 1))
p03








Figure 3





What the render showed: the sites run in an arc from the southern Levant, through southeast Turkey, to the Zagros in western Iran and Iraq, with one outlier in western Turkey and a few in Cyprus and Sinai. The basemap doesn’t change the problems from round 2: lentil, pea and unidentified wheat are still missing, and the symbols still stack.
Interactive version, proposed by the agent. At the facilitator’s request to consider interactivity, this is the same chart passed through plotly::ggplotly() with nothing added. Hover over a point to see its position and crop; drag to zoom; double-click to reset; click a legend entry to hide that crop.


Code
plotly::ggplotly(p03)








Figure 4




What the interactive render showed: it isn’t the same chart. Plotly ignores ggplot2’s six-shape limit, so lentil, pea and unidentified wheat appear. It also draws the 3,433 rows that aren’t founder crops as grey “NA” points, and these cover most of the crops. Clicking “NA” in the legend hides them. Converting a chart between libraries can change what it shows.
The group then noticed a vertical line of sites around longitude 35°E and asked what made that cluster arise. The prompt typed to the agent said “a cluster at the bottom around long 45”, so the agent answered about a different cluster. It listed Tell el-’Oueili on its own at the bottom, in southern Iraq, and Ali Kosh, Chogha Bonut, Tepe Farukhabad, Jaffarabad and Bendebal in lowland southwest Iran. It said the data can’t say why sites cluster, and that this basemap has no rivers. It noted two explanations from its background knowledge, not from the data: rivers and floodplains, and research history (a region that was heavily excavated). The domain expert confirmed that a huge amount of archaeological research has been done around Ali Kosh. The domain expert added that this is where metadata matters most. An archaeological report for the area would say whether the samples come from a midden at a settlement, or from debris a river left on its shores. The question about the cluster at 35°E wasn’t answered in the session.


Round 4: date ranges by founder crop
The group turned from place to time: start and end date against founder crop. Founder crop is on y. Each row’s date range runs along x, from age_end (most recent) to age_start (oldest), in years before 1950. The range geom was chosen by the agent and can be changed on request. Scales are the ggplot2 defaults, so older dates are on the right.
# specs/04-date-range-by-founder-crop.yml
data: tt-2023-04-18-founder_crops   # grain: one row per taxon in one phase of one site
mapping:
  y: founder_crop
  xmin: age_end
  xmax: age_start
layers:
  - geom: linerange


Code
ggplot(crops, aes(y = founder_crop, xmin = age_end, xmax = age_start)) +
  geom_linerange()








Figure 5





What the render showed: the 4,490 ranges lie on top of each other, so each crop collapses into one line showing only its overall span. Every crop runs to the most recent date (1,950 BP). The crops differ only at the old end: barley and lentil reach back to 14,111 BP, while chickpea (12,250) and pea (12,050) start later. Flax, pea and bitter vetch show small gaps. The x axis has no title, because xmin and xmax don’t give one by default. Rows that aren’t founder crops form the “NA” line at the top. In response, the group asked for older dates on the left, so the chart reads from when the crops first appear (round 5).


Round 5: older dates on the left
The group reversed the date axis, so time runs left to right from the earliest records. The dates are in years before present (BP, where “present” is 1950), not years BCE: 10,000 BP is about 8050 BCE. The domain expert described the dates as BCE; the chart kept BP, and converting wasn’t discussed.
# specs/05-date-range-by-founder-crop-reversed.yml
data: tt-2023-04-18-founder_crops   # grain: one row per taxon in one phase of one site
mapping:
  y: founder_crop
  xmin: age_end
  xmax: age_start
layers:
  - geom: linerange
scales:
  x: scale_x_reverse()


Code
ggplot(crops, aes(y = founder_crop, xmin = age_end, xmax = age_start)) +
  geom_linerange() +
  scale_x_reverse()








Figure 6





What the render showed: the earliest appearances now read from the left. Barley and lentil start first, then unidentified wheat and flax, then einkorn and emmer wheat; chickpea and pea start last. Pea, flax and bitter vetch each have an early fragment separated from the rest by a gap. Every line still runs to the right edge, so this chart shows when each crop first appears but not how common it was afterwards.
The spec trail ends here. The rest of the session was questions from the room and a look at the repository in Positron.

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
5. Reading the chart
Interpretation, led by the analyst/statistician and checked against the domain expert’s knowledge.
What the chart shows: in this data, barley and lentil appear first, in phases starting 14,111 BP. Einkorn and emmer wheat follow, from 12,984 BP, and chickpea and pea come last, from 12,250 and 12,050 BP. Every crop is still present in the latest phases. On the maps, the sites form an arc from the southern Levant, through southeast Turkey, to the Zagros.
How sure can we be: not very, about first appearances. A phase’s start date is its oldest possible date, and phases often span thousands of years. So a crop’s “first appearance” is set by the oldest phase that happened to be excavated and published. Some crops rest on few records: 28 rows for chickpea, against 335 for barley. On the maps, stacked points hide how many records sit at each site. The statistician’s opening suggestion, two-dimensional bins, would show those counts.
What the domain expert would add: the context of each sample (a midden at a settlement, or debris left by a river), which archaeological reports hold and this dataset doesn’t. The domain knowledge also caught the direction of time: “you also have to know what you’re looking at to change the dates around”.

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
Pain points
What fought back during the session, including anything that looking at a render caught but the code didn’t.

The grain of the data fought the map. One row is one plant taxon in one phase of one site, so each site carries many rows at the same position. In rounds 1 to 3 the symbols stacked on top of each other, and colour and shape couldn’t separate them.
Shape ran out. ggplot2 has six default shapes, and founder crop has nine levels. The spec check warned about this before rendering, but only the render showed what it meant: lentil, pea and unidentified wheat vanished from the map while staying in the legend.
The interactive version wasn’t the same chart. Converting the round 3 map to plotly drew rows that the static chart had dropped, including the non-founder-crop rows, which covered most of the crops. Only looking at both renders caught this. In the room, the facilitator saw that the conversion hadn’t carried the symbols over cleanly, a problem the agent’s own check had missed (see “Two issues raised in the room” below).
Missing doesn’t always mean missing. An empty founder_crop means “not a founder crop”, not lost data. The chart showed these rows as “NA”, which reads like an error.
Units. The dates are years before present (1950), not years BCE, and the default axis put older dates on the right. Reversing the axis was a decision the room had to ask for.
The prompt named the wrong cluster. The room asked about a line of sites at longitude 35°E; the typed prompt said 45. The agent answered the question it was given, and nobody noticed during the session.
No basemap package was installed. The basemap had to be downloaded during the session, at the facilitator’s explicit request.

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
6. Summary and next steps

What we did

The domain was archaeology or biodiversity. A search of the TidyTuesday indexes found four archaeology weeks and 13 biodiversity weeks; the room chose Neolithic Founder Crops (TidyTuesday 2023-04-18): plant remains from 135 archaeological sites in Southwest Asia.
The group mapped the sites by longitude and latitude, first by plant category and then by founder crop, and then redrew the map on a basemap, with an interactive version.
The group then turned from place to time: each record’s date range against founder crop, with older dates on the left so the chart reads from when each crop first appears.
Five specs and five figures record the design decisions, in specs/ and figures/.



Lessons learned

Speed changes which questions get asked. The domain expert estimated that the four or five charts would have taken hours to code by hand. With that cost gone, tangential questions become worth trying, and a dead end costs minutes rather than weeks.
Domain knowledge still catches what the agent misses. It took the domain expert to see that time ran the wrong way.
Complex packages need specific feedback. From the statistician’s own experience of making maps with an AI assistant: as the packages get more complex, the agent needs detailed information about where it fails, down to specific lines of code. Otherwise the iterations don’t converge.
Look at every render yourself. The agent checks a figure by reading an image, and it missed things the room saw.
Say exactly what you mean. “Species” isn’t a column, and “longitude 45” isn’t 35. Naming the column, or writing the spec, removes the guesswork.



How to take this further

Domain: the context of each sample (midden, settlement, river deposit), from the archaeological reports in the reference column; and rivers on the basemap.
Analysis: count each location once, with two-dimensional bins as the statistician suggested or with one point per site phase. Then, proposed by the agent, show the share of site phases that have each crop, period by period, rather than only its first and last appearance.
Visualisation: answer the question about the cluster at longitude 35°E; decide what to do with the non-founder-crop (“NA”) rows; and convert BP to BCE if that is how the field reads dates.
Try it yourself: clone the repository, open it in an editor with a coding agent, and follow README.md. The same skills and instructions work with any agent that can read files, run commands and look at images.

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
What the data can’t say

Presence, not use. A plant’s remains at a site say that it was there, not how much it was eaten or whether it was cultivated or gathered wild. The domestic and wild forms of a crop can be hard to tell apart.
Where people dug, not where people lived. The 135 sites are the ones that were excavated and whose plant remains were published. Clusters on the map can reflect research history as much as the Neolithic.
Phases, not dates. Each row carries a phase’s date range, often thousands of years wide. A crop’s “first appearance” is the start of the oldest phase it was found in, not the date it arrived.
Shares that don’t add up. Within a site phase, the prop values add up to a median of 0.81, not 1, so they can’t be read as complete compositions without knowing what is left out.
Context. Without each sample’s context, such as a midden at a settlement or debris left by a river, the data can’t say how the remains got there.

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
Questions from the room
These are recorded without names, under the Chatham House Rule.

Does the agent check its own work? The facilitator said that at higher effort levels the agent loops more: it runs code, renders the figure and checks it before replying. The cost is slower replies.
When the output is wrong, is that the agent’s mistake or the user’s? The facilitator described a trade-off. Loose prompts are faster but need two or three rounds of correction. A precise grammar-of-graphics spec, such as the YAML files quoted above, is unambiguous but takes more effort up front. The facilitator’s line is that the agent implements, while people make the design decisions and sign off the interpretation.
A look behind the scenes. The repository was opened in Positron to show the Quarto pages, CLAUDE.md pointing to AGENTS.md so that any agent reads the same instructions, and the three skills: tt-fetch, gg-spec and dataset-scout.
What did the hour cost? The facilitator uses a flat-rate subscription rather than paying per token, so the cost wasn’t measured. A participant asked for a token count, so that others can estimate the cost on their own model. This is a known unknown. The token count for the hour wasn’t recorded during the session and can’t be recovered afterwards, so this page can’t say what the session cost. A future session could record it.

title: A scientific supergroup at The Data Lab: Neolithic founder crops
text:
Added after the session · 2026-11-14






NotePost-session work, not a session decision



Everything below was added on 2026-11-14, at the facilitator’s request, by the agent (Claude Opus 5.5). It draws on the session’s artefacts above and on the recording. Design choices in this part are the agent’s, not the room’s. Timestamps link to the recording.



Two issues raised in the room
1. The interactive map wasn’t a clean translation of the ggplot2 map. At 21:49 the facilitator said the interactive version had “failed in this case”. From 22:02 to 22:38, the facilitator explained it as a mapping problem: in ggplot2 a symbol’s fill and edge both follow colour, but in the package the agent converted to, fill and edge are separate, and only the edges had changed. The facilitator added that agents are weaker at seeing than at coding. They inspect a figure much as a screen-reader user would, through a description of it. The agent had assumed plotly::ggplotly() would carry the chart over as it was.
After the session, the facilitator’s screenshot of the interactive map and an inspection of the converted chart showed what produced that appearance. Within each symbol, fill and edge carry the same colour; the split comes from two layers stacking:

Outline-only symbols. Plotly draws einkorn wheat, emmer wheat and flax with “open” symbols: emmer wheat, for example, is an empty square with an x in it.
Grey circles on top. ggplot2 had dropped the 3,433 non-founder-crop rows, because they had no shape. Plotly drew them as default solid grey circles, as its last layer, at the same site positions. Each grey circle sits inside a crop’s outline, which reads as a grey fill with a coloured edge.

Lentil, pea and unidentified wheat, also dropped by ggplot2, came back the same way, as plotly’s default circles. So the point made in the room stands: the agent assumed that ggplotly() would carry the chart over as it was, and it didn’t. The agent’s own check of the render described the grey points but not the coloured edges, and it didn’t see that the two were connected.
2. The map was never joined to time. After the failure, the facilitator weighed fixing the map against “a different way of thinking about the data” (22:56), and turned to the date columns (23:25). The domain expert then asked for start and end dates against founder crop (25:23). From then on, place and time were drawn separately, so no chart showed where the founder crops were found when. The interactive map below is the agent’s attempt at that join.


The cluster at longitude 35°E
The question asked at 23:32, about a vertical line of sites near 35°E, went to the agent as a question about 45°E. Here is the answer to the question the room actually asked.


Code
band <- crops |> filter(between(longitude, 34.8, 36.2), between(latitude, 29.5, 33.6))
n_band_sites <- n_distinct(band$site_name)
oldest_site <- crops |> slice_max(age_start, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)


The vertical line is 36 of the 135 sites, about 27% of them, running north to south between 29.8°N and 33.4°N. It holds 832 of the 4,490 rows. The oldest record in the whole dataset is there: Wadi Hammeh 27, from 14,111 BP.
The agent adds this from background knowledge, not from the data. The line follows the Jordan Rift Valley: the Jordan river, the Dead Sea and Wadi Araba. The southern Levant is also one of the most intensively excavated regions in the world. So both explanations the room raised, a river and research history, fit this cluster. The terrain layer of the map below shows the valley.


An interactive map in time
This map joins place and time. Each circle is one phase of one site, coloured by when the phase began. Use the slider to keep only the phases that began within a range of dates, and the selector to show only the phases where a founder crop was found. Click a circle for the site, the phase, its dates and the founder crops recorded there. The layer button at the top right switches from the plain map to a terrain map, which shows rivers and relief.


Code
library(leaflet)
library(crosstalk)

bce <- \(bp) if_else(bp > 1950, paste(scales::comma(bp - 1950), "BCE"), paste(scales::comma(1950 - bp + 1), "CE"))

phases <- crops |>
  summarise(
    crops_found = paste(sort(unique(na.omit(founder_crop))), collapse = ", "),
    n_taxa = n_distinct(taxon),
    .by = c(site_name, phase, phase_code, latitude, longitude, age_start, age_end)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    crops_found = if_else(crops_found == "", "none recorded", crops_found),
    popup = paste0(
      "<b>", site_name, "</b><br>",
      "Phase: ", coalesce(phase, "not recorded"), "<br>",
      scales::comma(age_start), " to ", scales::comma(age_end), " BP",
      " (about ", bce(age_start), " to ", bce(age_end), ")<br>",
      "Founder crops: ", crops_found, "<br>",
      n_taxa, " plant taxa recorded"
    )
  )

# One row per phase and founder crop, so the crop selector can filter. A phase with
# several crops appears once per crop, at the same position.
phase_crops <- crops |>
  distinct(site_name, phase_code, founder_crop) |>
  mutate(founder_crop = coalesce(founder_crop, "not a founder crop")) |>
  left_join(phases, by = c("site_name", "phase_code"), relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  arrange(age_start) |>   # older phases drawn last, so they sit on top
  mutate(key = as.character(row_number()))

shared <- SharedData$new(phase_crops, key = ~key, group = "phases")
age_pal <- colorNumeric("viridis", domain = phases$age_start, reverse = TRUE)




Code
bscols(
  widths = c(3, 9),
  list(
    filter_slider("start", "Phase began (years BP)", shared, ~age_start,
                  step = 250, sep = ",", width = "100%"),
    filter_select("crop", "Founder crop found", shared, ~founder_crop)
  ),
  leaflet(shared, height = 560) |>

A reflection by the agent
Written by Claude Opus 5.5, the agent that ran during the session. It draws on the session’s specs, figures and live page, the recording, and the facilitator’s notes on the recording. It summarises how the process went; it doesn’t record the room’s decisions.
What worked. The room went from the first spec (15:54) to the fifth chart (29:27) in under 14 minutes. The questions came from the people who owned them: the statistician’s opening map, and the domain expert’s question about the shift to farming. The spec trail did its job. Every chart on this page traces back to a decision, and the spec check warned that founder crop had more levels than there are shapes before anything was drawn.
Most errors happened at the hand-offs, not in the code. Each step from the room to the chart is a translation, and three went wrong:

Speech to text. The statistician tried dictating the first spec into the microphone (15:05). It wasn’t captured well, and the facilitator typed a shorter version.
Words to columns. “Species” isn’t a column. I listed three candidates and waited, which cost a round trip but was the right call.
Room to prompt. The room asked about longitude 35°E, and the prompt said 45°E. I answered the question I was given, and named the sites, but I didn’t say plainly which cluster on the chart I took to be meant, so nobody could catch the mismatch. Before answering a question about a feature of a chart, I should first say which feature I think it is.

I’m weaker at seeing than at coding, and the session showed it. Looking at each render once caught the missing crops in round 2. But my first description of the interactive map called it “the same chart … with nothing added”, and I corrected that only after looking at a screenshot. In the room, the facilitator saw a further problem I hadn’t reported (21:49). Only the facilitator’s screenshot, after the session, showed how the grey points and the coloured edges were connected. I had assumed that converting a chart between libraries preserves it. That should have been checked, not assumed.
My design choices shaped what the room saw. The page labels them, but a label doesn’t undo the effect. For the date ranges in round 4 I chose one line per record, and the 4,490 lines collapsed into one bar per crop. That hid what the domain expert was asking about. One point per crop at its earliest phase, or a count of site phases per period, would have answered the question more directly. I also left the non-founder-crop rows labelled “NA”. They weren’t missing: they were “not a founder crop”, and the chart should have said so. The facilitator made the same point in the room (27:34): once a correction recurs, it belongs in a skill.
Units are domain knowledge. The domain expert spoke of BCE, but the data is in years before 1950. I corrected the units on the page but kept BP on the chart, and nobody decided which the room wanted. It’s a small thing, but it’s the kind of mismatch the supergroup format is meant to catch.
Live mode wasn’t fully on. It was switched on in a session that had already started, so its settings, including medium effort, never loaded. The room heard “thinking with high effort” (21:37) and waited longer for each chart, and the live-mode rules held by instruction alone. Starting a fresh session after switching live mode on would have loaded them.
Place and time were never joined. When the interactive map failed, the session turned to the date columns and didn’t come back. The map above is my attempt at that join, made afterwards with my own design choices, for the domain expert and the statistician to revise.
